title: Raga Asa
hook: the raga of hope, and the ballad sung while the sky is still dark

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hymn in Gauri: Sukhmani, peace built section by section, and your line was peace in gauri. A new week starts now.

Long before sunrise, the street outside a gurdwara is still dark, a dog barks somewhere, and a few cars pull in with their headlights on. Inside, the lights are already up. Someone uncovers a harmonium. A tabla player taps the drumhead, listening for the pitch. People drift in with their heads covered, sit on the carpet, and the singing begins before the birds do. What they're singing has a name: the Asa di Var, the ballad in Asa.
screen: `STILL DARK OUTSIDE.` → `THE SINGING STARTS FIRST.` → `THE BALLAD IN ASA.`

segments.voice: Raga Asa is the next great section of the Guru Granth Sahib, right after Gauri. In Punjabi, asa is also an everyday word for hope, and Sikh tradition likes to hear that in the raga's name: the raga of hope. Its mood is described as longing that leans forward, a hope that something good is on its way. That fits the hour. By Sikh custom the Asa di Var belongs to the morning, sung in gurdwaras while the day is still breaking. A var is a ballad, built of stanzas called pauris, with short verses called saloks set between them. In this one, the saloks come from Guru Nanak and Guru Angad. Here's one of Guru Angad's, in plain English. If a hundred moons rose, and a thousand suns climbed the sky, with all that light there would still be deep darkness without the Guru. Heard at dawn, that lands differently. The sun is coming up anyway; the salok says outside light isn't the whole story. There's a light the Sikh Gurus point to that a sunrise can't supply, the light of the Guru's word. So the ballad is sung right at the edge of morning, while one kind of light is arriving, to ask for the other. Hope at dawn, then, isn't forced cheer. It's facing the day before it has shown its hand, and starting it with the Word.
screen: `ASA: THE RAGA OF HOPE.` · `SUNG AS THE DAY BREAKS.` · `A HUNDRED MOONS, A THOUSAND SUNS.` · `STILL DARK WITHOUT THE GURU.` · then, large: `HOPE AT DAWN.`

segments.voice: Let your breath slow and picture the sky just before sunrise, not dark, not light, that gray-blue in between. Let one real hope come up, small or large, for today or for someone you love, and let it sit there in the half-light without polishing it. If you pray, say Waheguru once and leave the hope with it; if you don't, keep it company quietly.
Raga Asa. The raga tradition hears as hope, home of the Asa di Var, the ballad sung while the morning breaks. Today's word.

chat.says: Why do gurdwaras sing the Asa di Var before sunrise?
options: By custom it's the morning ballad: Asa is hope, asking for the Guru's light as day breaks.
The Gurus forbade singing it after sunrise, so the whole ballad always has to end by dawn.
It's a hymn about the sun, praising sunrise as the source of all light.
